extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism and mass communication; reporters, editors, and news graphic designers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating journalistic infographics that combine data, text, and graphics to explain complex information quickly and clearly. Emphasises design choices, narrative, accuracy, and medium-appropriate formats for newsroom use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose / goal
rubrics_metrics.description: An infographic is a visual representation of information, data, or knowledge designed to present complex ideas quickly and clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for rapid comprehension and memory: blend text, images, icons, and graphical elements so the core idea is understandable at a glance rather than requiring a spreadsheet of numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and content (accuracy & relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every infographic starts with reliable information: numerical data (statistics, survey results, financial figures) or qualitative content (processes, timelines, comparisons). The data forms the backbone of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a strong underlying structure that controls narrative flow and preserves data integrity. Choose only relevant data that serves the story; irrelevant facts weaken the infographic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (sourcing and verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every statistic, data point, and claim must be sourced and verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite sources visibly where appropriate. A beautiful infographic built on bad or unsourced data is worse than none. Verification is the top priority before design choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (immediate message)
rubrics_metrics.description: The infographic's message should be immediately apparent; readers should understand the point within a few seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If viewers must spend more than a few seconds figuring out what they're looking at, the design has failed. Use clear headlines, captions, and annotations to orient readers quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity (remove nonessential elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity means removing everything that doesn't serve the story; not dumbing down the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary decoration, excessive text, and competing colours. Keep only elements that contribute to the narrative or comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual hierarchy (guide the eye)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual hierarchy determines how the reader's eye moves through the information in the intended order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the most important point the most visually prominent, with supporting information arranged in descending emphasis. Use size, contrast, colour, and placement to establish priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual elements & chart selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts, graphs, icons, illustrations, maps, and photographs translate raw information into scannable visuals; the choice of element must match the data and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select charts to match the data: pie charts for proportions, timelines for change over time, maps for geographic data. Icons can replace lengthy labels to increase scannability. Mismatched chart types confuse rather than clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text and typography (readability and hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Text supports visuals through headlines, captions, annotations, and short paragraphs; typography choices influence readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a clear typographic hierarchy (title, subheads, body). Limit fonts to two or three: one for the title, another for subheadings, and a clean font for body text. Pay attention to size, spacing, and legibility at the intended reproduction size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour and layout (palette and flow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour sets tone and guides the eye; layout determines how information flows across the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a restrained palette (typically two to three complementary colours) rather than many competing hues. Arrange elements to work with natural reading patterns (upper-left to lower-right) and place key information where the eye lands first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative structure (storytelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: An infographic should tell a story with a beginning (hook/headline), middle (supporting data/evidence), and end (takeaway or call to action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence sections and visual emphasis to support the narrative. Every design choice — order, colour emphasis, highlighted statistics — should serve the story arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose & audience fit (infographic vs data visualization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographics are built for communication and often persuasion for a broad audience; data visualizations focus on objective representation and exploration, often for analysts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the project needs a narrative-driven infographic (to explain implications to a general audience) or an exploratory data visualization (to let users interrogate data). Match interactivity, complexity, and wording to the intended audience's needs and expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactivity & medium suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Data visualizations are frequently interactive (digital); infographics are typically static images but can be interactive, animated, or immersive depending on the platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose format based on distribution: static for print and shareable social images; interactive or animated for web and social video. Consider emerging formats (interactive infographics, AR) when appropriate for audience engagement and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis and revealing relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographics can reveal patterns and relationships by combining multiple datasets and using visual cues to link them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual proximity, consistent colour coding, annotations, and juxtaposition to show correlations or causal relationships across datasets. The goal is to let viewers see how separate pieces of information connect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate infographic type
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of infographics suit different information: statistical, informational, timeline, comparison, process, geographic, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the type to the story: statistical for survey/demographic data; informational for explaining concepts; timeline for chronological events; comparison for side-by-side evaluations; process for step-by-step flows; geographic for map-based data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and workflow (maestro concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collaborative newsroom workflow — where writers, editors, designers, and data specialists work together from story inception — improves infographic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate designers and data experts early to align narrative goals with visual strategy and data integrity. Use a 'maestro' approach to coordinate roles and keep the visual and textual elements coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement (hold attention and aid recall)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good infographic engages viewers, using design and narrative to hold attention and improve information recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ compelling hooks, careful use of colour and layout, and a clear narrative to make readers want to keep looking. Research (e.g., Journal of Visual Literacy) shows well-designed infographics improve recall and experience.
